question:
(i) State Ohm's Law and explain the condition under which a conductor obeys it.
(ii) Compare the $V-I$ characteristics of an ohmic conductor and a semiconductor diode. Why is a semiconductor diode called a non-ohmic device?

options.A:
(i) Ohm's law states $V=IR$ under all temperatures and physical conditions.
(ii) Both an ohmic conductor and a diode have a straight-line $V-I$ graph through the origin, so both are ohmic.
options.B:
(i) Ohm's law states $V\propto\dfrac{1}{I}$ at constant temperature.
(ii) A diode has constant resistance in forward and reverse bias and therefore obeys Ohm's law.
options.C:
(i) At constant temperature and unchanged physical conditions, current is proportional to voltage: $V=IR$.
(ii) An ohmic conductor has a linear $V-I$ graph through the origin and constant resistance. A diode has a nonlinear, directional characteristic: appreciable current in forward bias after barrier reduction and very small reverse current. Therefore it is non-ohmic.
options.D:
(i) Ohm's law applies only when a conductor is heated continuously.
(ii) A diode is non-ohmic because its current is always zero for every applied voltage.
